stem:
Which corneal layer constitutes approximately 90% of the total corneal thickness and is composed of regularly
arranged collagen lamellae?
rationale: Stroma (substantia propria) forms 90% of total corneal thickness.

stem:
A 45-year-old farmer presents with eye pain, photophobia, and decreased vision 3 days after being struck by a
tree branch. Slit-lamp exam shows a central corneal ulcer with feathery margins and satellite lesions. What is the drug of
choice?
rationale:
Fungal keratitis after vegetative trauma presents with feathery margins & satellite lesions; Natamycin 5% is
1st-line.

stem:
A 22-year-old man presents with a foreign body sensation and photophobia. Fluorescein staining reveals a
branching dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs. Corneal sensation is reduced. Which medication is STRICTLY
CONTRAINDICATED?
rationale:
Topical steroids are strictly contraindicated in active HSV dendritic keratitis due to risk of geographical
ulceration/perforation.

stem:
A 20-year-old contact lens wearer who admits to washing her lenses with tap water presents with severe ocular
pain disproportionate to clinical findings. Examination shows a ring-shaped corneal infiltrate and radial keratoneuritis. What is
the most likely pathogen?
rationale:
Acanthamoeba causes severe pain disproportionate to signs, ring infiltrate, & radial keratoneuritis in contact
lens users.

stem:
A 18-year-old male with progressive astigmatism shows a V-shaped indentation of his lower eyelid on
downgaze (Munson's sign) and fine vertical stress lines in the deep stroma. What is the investigation of choice to detect early
ectasia?
rationale: Pentacam / Corneal Topography is the gold standard for early keratoconus detection.

stem:
Which layer of the cornea acts as an active Na+/K+-ATPase metabolic dehydration pump to maintain corneal
deturgescence and transparency, but possesses NO regenerative capacity?
rationale: Endothelium acts as Na+/K+-ATPase pump to maintain deturgescence & cannot regenerate.

stem:
A patient presents with a dense white corneal opacity involving the full thickness of the stroma with iris adherent
to its posterior surface following a healed perforated ulcer. What is the correct clinical designation?
rationale: Full thickness opacity with iris adherent posteriorly = Adherent leucoma.

stem:
A 30-year-old patient presents with recurrent corneal erosion syndrome. Histological examination shows
damage to Bowman's layer. Which statement regarding Bowman's layer is correct?

options.A: It is an active metabolic fluid pump
options.B: It cannot regenerate and heals by fibrous scar tissue

rationale: Bowman's layer cannot regenerate and heals by scarring.

stem:
Which of the following organisms possesses the unique ability to penetrate intact, healthy corneal epithelium
without requiring a prior epithelial defect?
rationale: Neisseria gonorrhoeae can invade intact corneal epithelium.

stem:
A 65-year-old female presents with morning blurring of vision that improves as the day progresses. Slit-lamp
examination reveals corneal guttae and endothelial decompensation. What is the diagnosis?
rationale: Fuchs' dystrophy shows endothelial guttae & morning blurring due to nocturnal corneal swelling.

stem:
A patient with bilateral corneal clouding undergoes genetic testing confirming an Autosomal Recessive
inheritance pattern. Which corneal dystrophy exhibits Autosomal Recessive inheritance?
rationale:
Macular stromal dystrophy is Autosomal Recessive (Mnem: Macular = Recessive; Granular/Lattice =
Dominant).

stem:
In a patient undergoing Corneal Collagen Cross-Linking (C3R) for progressive keratoconus, which vitamin
photo-sensitizer and ultraviolet radiation wavelength are used?
rationale: C3R uses Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) and UV-A light (365 nm) to stiffen collagen.

stem:
A 35-year-old patient with a non-healing neurotrophic corneal ulcer secondary to CN V1 trigeminal nerve palsy
is scheduled for protective lid closure. Which type of tarsorrhaphy preserves central vision?
rationale: Lateral tarsorrhaphy fuses outer 1/3 of eyelids, maintaining central visual axis.

stem:
Which type of corneal graft procedure involves replacing only the anterior layers of the cornea down to
Descemet's membrane while preserving the patient's native host endothelium?
rationale: DALK replaces anterior stroma down to Descemet's while preserving native host endothelium.

stem:
A patient presents with a ring of copper deposition at the periphery of the cornea in Descemet's membrane
(Kayser-Fleischer ring). In which condition is this pathognomonic?
rationale: Kayser-Fleischer ring (copper in Descemet's) is pathognomonic for Wilson's disease.

stem:
What is the primary refractive power provided by the anterior surface of the human cornea in an emmetropic
eye?
rationale: Cornea provides ~43 D of the eye's total ~60 D refractive power.

stem:
A 16-year-old boy with poorly controlled Type 1 Diabetes presents with rapid bilateral vision reduction. Slit-lamp
exam reveals acute white cortical opacities. What named cataract pattern is this?
rationale: Snowflake / Snowstorm cataract is characteristic of uncontrolled Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.

stem:
An infant presents with bilateral central lens opacities showing an 'oil-droplet' appearance. Laboratory screening
reveals reducing substances in the urine. What is the underlying diagnosis?
rationale: Oil-droplet cataract + urine reducing substances = Galactosemia.

stem:
A 50-year-old patient with myotonic dystrophy is found to have iridescent, multi-colored crystalline opacities in the
deep cortex and nucleus of the lens. What is this cataract called?
rationale: Myotonic dystrophy causes Christmas-tree iridescent cataract.

stem:
A patient with long-standing systemic corticosteroid therapy for rheumatoid arthritis presents with severe glare
while driving in bright sunlight. Which type of cataract is specifically associated with chronic steroid use?
rationale: Chronic systemic or topical steroids cause Posterior Subcapsular Cataract (PSC).

stem:
What is the single most common late postoperative complication following uncomplicated phacoemulsification
with intraocular lens (IOL) implantation?
rationale: Posterior Capsule Opacification (PCO / Elschnig's pearls) is the most common late complication.

stem:
A 68-year-old patient who developed posterior capsule opacification (Elschnig's pearls) 1 year post-cataract
surgery undergoes laser therapy. Which laser is used for capsulotomy?
rationale: Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy is the non-invasive treatment for PCO.

stem:
A 45-year-old male suffers blunt trauma to his right eye from a tennis ball. Examination reveals a ring of iris
pigment imprinted on the anterior lens capsule. What is this sign?
rationale: Vossius' ring is iris pigment on anterior lens capsule post-blunt trauma.

stem:
In an aphakic patient whose crystalline lens was extracted without IOL placement, which Purkinje-Sanson
images are characteristically ABSENT on examination?
rationale: Aphakia causes loss of the 3rd (anterior lens) and 4th (posterior lens) Purkinje images.

stem:
A 2-year-old child presents with a congenital cataract. What is the most common morphological type of
congenital cataract encountered clinically?
rationale: Lamellar (zonular) cataract is the commonest congenital cataract type.

stem:
A patient with hypermature senile cataract presents with sudden pain and redness. The cortex has liquefied,
allowing the dense brown nucleus to sink to the bottom of the capsular bag. What is this cataract termed?
rationale: Morgagnian cataract occurs when liquefied cortex allows brown nucleus to sink inferiorly.

stem:
During phacoemulsification, a sudden deepening of the anterior chamber, pupil constriction, and loss of nuclear
fragment support occur. What intraoperative complication has taken place?
rationale: Deep AC, pupil constriction, & nuclear sink signify Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR).

stem:
In calculating intraocular lens (IOL) power using the SRK formula (P = A - 2.5B - 0.9C), what do parameters B
and C represent respectively?
rationale: SRK formula P = A - 2.5(Axial Length) - 0.9(Average K).

stem:
A 12-year-old boy presents with upward and temporal lens subluxation (ectopia lentis), high stature, and
arachnodactyly. What is the underlying genetic defect?
rationale: Marfan syndrome (Fibrillin-1) causes superior-temporal ectopia lentis.

stem:
A patient with homocystinuria presents with ectopia lentis. In which direction does the lens characteristically
displace in homocystinuria?
rationale: Homocystinuria causes downward and nasal ectopia lentis.

stem:
A 60-year-old hypermetropic female presents with excruciating eye pain, halo vision, fixed mid-dilated pupil,
and IOP of 62 mmHg. What is the mandatory immediate IV drug to lower IOP rapidly?
rationale: IV Mannitol 20% rapidly reduces vitreous volume & IOP in acute angle-closure emergency.

stem:
Following successful medical lowering of IOP in an acute angle-closure attack, what is the definitive
surgical procedure required in BOTH the affected and fellow eyes?
rationale: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) in BOTH eyes is definitive treatment for angle closure.

stem:
Which anti-glaucoma eye drop works by increasing uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor and is known to
cause iris hyperpigmentation and eyelash elongation?
rationale: Prostaglandins (Latanoprost) increase uveoscleral outflow, cause iris darkening & lash growth.

stem:
A 55-year-old glaucoma patient with a history of severe bronchial asthma requires topical anti-glaucoma
therapy. Which medication is STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED due to risk of fatal bronchospasm?
rationale: Timolol (non-selective beta blocker) is strictly contraindicated in asthma/COPD.

stem:
A 2-month-old infant presents with photophobia, epiphora, blepharospasm, and hazy enlarged corneas with
horizontal Descemet's breaks (Haab's striae). If the cornea is clear, what is the operation of choice?
rationale: Goniotomy is procedure of choice for congenital glaucoma if cornea is clear.

stem:
A 65-year-old male with Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG) exhibits visual field defects. What is the
arcuate visual field defect extending from the blind spot around fixation to the nasal hemifield called?
rationale: Bjerrum scotoma is an arcuate visual field defect extending around fixation.

stem:
In Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma, what is the major anatomical site of resistance to aqueous humor
outflow?
rationale: Juxtacanalicular trabecular meshwork is main site of resistance in POAG.

stem:
A patient presents with an IOP of 26 mmHg on multiple occasions, but optic disc examination reveals
normal cup-to-disc ratio (0.3) and visual fields are completely normal. What is the diagnosis?
rationale: IOP >21 mmHg without optic disc or visual field damage = Ocular Hypertension.

stem:
A 50-year-old patient exhibits optic nerve cupping (CDR 0.8) and arcuate scotomas on perimetry, but IOP
readings consistently remain below 21 mmHg. What is the diagnosis?
rationale: Glaucomatous disc/field damage with IOP <=21 mmHg = Normal Tension Glaucoma.

stem:
Slit-lamp examination of a myopic patient shows a vertical line of pigment deposited on the posterior
surface of the corneal endothelium. What is this sign called?
rationale: Krukenberg's spindle is endothelial vertical pigment line in pigmentary glaucoma.

stem:
During gonioscopy, hyperpigmentation is observed anterior to Schwalbe's line. What is this gonioscopic
landmark called?
rationale: Sampaolesi line is pigment line anterior to Schwalbe's line on gonioscopy.

stem:
A patient undergoes trabeculectomy for uncontrolled POAG. Which antimetabolite is applied
intraoperatively to prevent episcleral scarring and bleb failure?
rationale: Mitomycin-C / 5-FU prevent episcleral scarring after trabeculectomy.

stem:
A patient with advanced hypermature cataract presents with sudden IOP elevation to 45 mmHg.
Examination shows lens protein leakage through an intact capsule with macrophages engulfing lens debris in the AC. What is
the diagnosis?
rationale: Phacolytic glaucoma = lens protein leakage through intact capsule triggering macrophage response.

stem:
A patient with intumescent swollen cataract presents with acute angle closure due to pupillary block caused
by anteroposterior lens enlargement. What type of glaucoma is this?
rationale: Phacomorphic glaucoma = swollen intumescent lens causing secondary angle closure.

stem:
A 65-year-old hypertensive patient presents with sudden, complete, painless loss of vision. Fundoscopy shows
an opaque, pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea. What is the diagnosis?
rationale: Pale retina + cherry-red fovea + sudden vision loss = Central Retinal Artery Occlusion.

stem: What is the most common site of origin for an embolus causing Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)?
rationale: Carotid artery bifurcation emboli (Hollenhorst plaques) are commonest source for CRAO.

stem:
A 60-year-old male presents with sudden vision loss. Fundoscopy reveals widespread flame-shaped
hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, tortuous dilated veins, and cotton wool spots ('Blood-and-thunder' fundus). What is the
diagnosis?
rationale: Blood-and-thunder fundus (flame hemorrhages in 4 quadrants) = CRVO.

stem:
Which complication is classically associated with Ischemic CRVO, typically developing approximately 90
days after the primary vascular event ('100-day glaucoma')?
rationale: Ischemic CRVO predisposes to Neovascular Glaucoma around 90-100 days.

stem:
A diabetic patient exhibits neovascularization at the optic disc (NVD) and pre-retinal hemorrhages. What is the
definitive treatment to prevent severe visual loss?
rationale: Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) is definitive treatment for PDR.

stem:
A 50-year-old high myopic patient presents with sudden onset of flashes of light (photopsia), shower of floaters,
and a curtain-like shadow descending over visual field. What is the diagnosis?
rationale: Flashes, floaters, & curtain-like field loss = Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment.

stem:
On slit-lamp biomicroscopy of a patient with suspected retinal tear, brown pigment granules are observed
floating in the anterior vitreous ('Tobacco dust'). What is this pathognomonic sign called?
rationale: Shaffer's sign (tobacco dust) = vitreous pigment granules indicating retinal tear.

stem:
A 25-year-old night-blind patient demonstrates bone-spicule hyperpigmentation in the mid-peripheral retina,
arteriolar attenuation, and waxy disc pallor on fundoscopy. What is the diagnosis?
rationale: Night blindness + bone-spicule pigmentation + waxy disc pallor = Retinitis Pigmentosa.

stem:
A 18-month-old child is brought by parents who noticed a white pupillary reflex (Leukocoria) in the left eye. CT
scan reveals intraocular calcification. What is the most likely diagnosis?
rationale: Leukocoria + intraocular calcification on CT = Retinoblastoma.

stem: Which gene mutation is responsible for hereditary hereditary Retinoblastoma, located on chromosome 13q14?
rationale: RB1 gene on chromosome 13q14 is responsible for Retinoblastoma.

stem:
A patient with Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis (SBE) demonstrates pale-centered retinal microhemorrhages on
fundoscopy. What are these lesions termed?
rationale: Roth's spots are white-centered retinal hemorrhages seen in SBE & leukemia.

stem:
In a patient with hypertensive retinopathy, deflection of veins at arteriovenous crossings is observed. What is
this sign called?
rationale: Salus sign is AV deflection; Bonnet sign is distal venous engorgement.

stem:
Which type of Retinal Detachment occurs WITHOUT a full-thickness retinal break or vitreoretinal traction,
secondary to subretinal fluid accumulation from choroidal tumors or inflammation?
rationale: Exudative RD occurs without retinal break due to subretinal fluid accumulation.

stem:
What is the primary mechanism of action of intravitreal Anti-VEGF agents (e.g., Ranibizumab, Aflibercept,
Bevacizumab) in treating diabetic macular edema and PDR?

options.D: Inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor to decrease vascular permeability & angiogenesis

rationale: Anti-VEGF inhibits VEGF to reduce vascular permeability & neovascularization.

stem:
A premature infant born at 28 weeks gestation receiving high-concentration supplemental oxygen develops
fibrovascular proliferation at the avascular-vascular retinal junction. What is the diagnosis?
rationale: Prematurity + oxygen therapy + retinal vascular junction ridge = ROP.

stem:
Failure of the primary vitreous and fetal hyaloid vascular system to regress after the 7th month of gestation
leads to which congenital cause of leukocoria?
rationale: Persistent Hyperplastic Primary Vitreous (PHPV) = failure of hyaloid system regression.

stem:
A 30-year-old male with ankylosing spondylitis presents with acute painful red eye, photophobia, and miosis.
What is the EARLIEST clinical sign of anterior uveitis on slit-lamp exam?
rationale: Aqueous flare (protein leakage) is earliest sign of acute anterior uveitis.

stem:
Slit-lamp examination of a patient with granulomatous iridocyclitis shows large, greasy inflammatory deposits on
the corneal endothelium. What are these called?
rationale: Mutton-fat KPs (epithelioid cells) signify granulomatous uveitis.

stem:
A patient with anterior uveitis demonstrates inflammatory nodules located at the pupillary margin. What are these
nodules named?
rationale: Koeppe nodules lie at pupillary border; Busacca lie on iris stroma.

stem:
Inflammatory nodules located on the anterior surface of the iris stroma away from the pupil in granulomatous
uveitis are termed:
rationale: Busacca nodules are on anterior iris stroma away from pupil.

stem:
A 28-year-old female presents with chronic unilateral uveitis, heterochromia iridis, stellate KPs over the entire
endothelium, and cataract, but ABSENCE of posterior synechiae. What is the syndrome?
rationale: Fuchs' Heterochromic Iridocyclitis = heterochromia, stellate KPs, NO posterior synechiae.

stem:
A patient who suffered a penetrating ocular injury to the right eye 6 weeks ago now presents with bilateral
granulomatous panuveitis. What pathognomonic nodules are seen between RPE and Bruch's membrane?
rationale: Dalen-Fuchs nodules (RPE-Bruch's membrane) occur in Sympathetic Ophthalmitis.

stem:
Fundoscopy of an immunocompromised AIDS patient shows extensive white retinal necrosis with confluent
retinal hemorrhages ('Pizza-pie' or 'Ketchup' fundus). What is the pathogen?
rationale: CMV retinitis presents with pizza-pie / ketchup fundus in AIDS patients.

stem:
A 3-day-old neonate presents with severe bilateral eyelid edema and hyperacute profuse purulent
discharge. Gram stain reveals Gram-negative intracellular diplococci. What is the treatment?
rationale: Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis (days 2-5) requires Systemic Cefotaxime/Ceftriaxone.

stem:
A 10-day-old infant presents with mucopurulent conjunctivitis. Giemsa stain of conjunctival scrapings
shows basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies. What is the pathogen and treatment?
rationale: Chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum (days 5-14) presents with inclusion bodies; give oral Erythromycin.

stem:
A 10-year-old boy presents with severe itching, ropy discharge, cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal
conjunctiva, and Horner-Trantas spots at the limbus. What is the diagnosis?
rationale: Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) presents with cobblestone papillae & Horner-Trantas spots.

stem:
A patient from an endemic region exhibits linear conjunctival scarring on the superior tarsal conjunctiva
(Arlt's line) and healed limbal depressions (Herbert's pits). What is the diagnosis?

options.C: Trachoma (Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A, B, Ba, C)

rationale: Arlt's line (tarsal scar) & Herbert's pits (limbal depressions) = Trachoma.

stem:
A 6-year-old malnourished child exhibits foamy triangular keratinized patches on the temporal bulbar
conjunctiva (Bitot's spots) and night blindness. What deficiency is present?
rationale: Bitot's spots (foamy keratin patches) = Vitamin A deficiency.

stem:
A patient presents with a fleshy, wing-shaped fibrovascular conjunctival growth encroaching onto the
nasal cornea crossing Bowman's membrane. What is this condition called?
rationale: Pterygium is wing-shaped fibrovascular conjunctival growth crossing limbus.

stem:
An elderly patient presents with a localized nodular swelling of the eyelid margin accompanied by loss of
eyelashes (madarosis) and destruction of Meibomian orifices. Biopsy reveals sebaceous gland carcinoma. What characteristic
spread pattern does it exhibit?
rationale: Sebaceous gland carcinoma exhibits Pagetoid epithelial spread.

stem:
A 45-year-old patient presents with progressive loss of peripheral vision in both eyes. Automated perimetry
demonstrates bitemporal hemianopia. Where is the underlying lesion?
rationale: Optic chiasm lesion compresses decussating nasal fibers causing bitemporal hemianopia.

stem: A patient with a lesion involving the right optic tract will display which characteristic visual field defect?
rationale: Right optic tract lesion causes contralateral (Left) homonymous hemianopia.

stem:
A patient with a stroke involving the temporal lobe optic radiation (Meyer's loop) displays which characteristic
visual field loss?

options.B: Superior homonymous quadrantanopia ('Pie in the sky')
options.D: Inferior homonymous quadrantanopia ('Pie on the floor')

rationale: Meyer's loop (temporal lobe) lesion causes Superior homonymous quadrantanopia (Pie in sky).

stem:
A 56-year-old diabetic male presents with sudden diplopia and right ptosis. The right eye is deviated 'down and
out'. Pupillary light reflexes are normal and equal in both eyes (pupil-sparing). What is the cause?
rationale: Diabetic microvascular 3rd nerve palsy causes pupil-sparing down-and-out eye deviation.

stem:
During the swinging flashlight test, when light is moved from the normal left eye to the affected right eye, both
pupils paradoxically dilate. What is this sign called?

options.E: Marcus Gunn pupil (Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect / RAPD)

rationale: Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD) dilates paradoxically during swinging flashlight test.

stem:
A patient presents with bilateral small, irregular pupils that do NOT react to light but react briskly to
accommodation (Light-Near Dissociation). What is this classic pupil associated with neurosyphilis called?
rationale: Argyll Robertson pupil shows Light-Near Dissociation (neurosyphilis).

stem:
A 6-year-old child presents with severe congenital ptosis. Levator function is measured at 2 mm (poor levator
action). Bell's phenomenon is present. What is the operation of choice?
rationale: Frontalis sling surgery is indicated in severe ptosis with poor levator function (<4 mm).

stem:
A patient with mild ptosis (1.5 mm) and good levator function (10 mm) is scheduled for surgical correction.
Which surgical procedure resects a portion of tarsus, conjunctiva, and Müller's muscle from behind the lid?
rationale: Fasanella-Servat resects tarsus, conjunctiva, & Müller's muscle for mild ptosis.

stem:
An 80-year-old patient presents with involutional entropion of the lower eyelid where the lid margin rolls inward
causing cilia to rub against the cornea. Which muscle instability is primarily responsible?

options.D: Overriding of capsulopalpebral fascia / inferior resected aponeurosis & orbicularis oculi

rationale: Involutional entropion is caused by overriding orbicularis oculi & lower resected aponeurosis.

stem:
A patient presents with a painful, acute focal staphylococcal infection of the lash follicle and associated Glands
of Zeis or Moll. What is the clinical term for an external hordeolum?
rationale: External hordeolum (Stye) is acute staphylococcal infection of Zeis/Moll glands.

stem:
A 10-month-old infant presents with epiphora from the right eye since birth. Pressing over the lacrimal sac
yields mucopurulent discharge. Digital lacrimal massage has failed. What is the next step?

options.A: Nasolacrimal duct probing under general anesthesia

rationale: Nasolacrimal duct probing under GA is 2nd-line for failed CNLDO massage after 6-12 mos.

stem:
In congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (CNLDO), what is the most common anatomical site of
membrane obstruction?
rationale: Valve of Hasner at inferior meatus is most common site of CNLDO membrane.

stem:
A 50-year-old female presents with a painful, red, swollen mass over the medial canthus below the medial
palpebral ligament with purulent discharge. What is the diagnosis?
rationale: Acute Dacryocystitis is acute painful infection of lacrimal sac below medial palpebral lig.

stem:
A worker splashes quicklime (alkali) into his eye. What is the mandatory FIRST intervention required before
performing any detailed examination or vision test?

options.A: Immediate copious eye irrigation with normal saline or clean water for 15-30 mins

rationale: Copious eye irrigation for 15-30 mins takes absolute priority in chemical burns.

stem:
Which type of chemical injury is MORE DESTRUCTIVE to ocular tissues due to saponification of cell
membranes and deep tissue penetration?
rationale: Alkali burns cause liquefactive necrosis & cell saponification, penetrating deeply.

stem:
A patient struck in the eye with a fist presents with double vision on upward gaze, enophthalmos, and
numbness over the right cheek (infraorbital nerve hypoesthesia). Which orbital wall is fractured?
rationale: Orbital floor (maxillary bone) is thinnest and most commonly fractured in blow-out injury.

stem:
A patient's parallel rays of light enter the unaccommodated eye and focus in front of the retina. What refractive
error is present and which lens corrects it?
rationale: Myopia focuses light in front of retina and is corrected by Concave (minus) lens.

stem:
A 45-year-old patient experiences gradual difficulty reading fine print at near distance due to age-related loss of
lens elasticity. What is this condition called?
rationale: Presbyopia is age-related loss of accommodation/lens elasticity after 40.

stem:
What is a difference in the refractive power between the two eyes exceeding 2.0 Diopters termed, which
predisposes young children to amblyopia?
rationale: Anisometropia is refractive power difference between eyes >2.0 D.

stem:
A 4-year-old child presents with inward deviation of the right eye (Esotropia). Cover-uncover test confirms
manifest squint. What is the primary cause of accommodative esotropia in children?
rationale: Accommodative esotropia is driven by excessive convergence induced by uncorrected hypermetropia.

stem:
Which extraocular muscle is isolated and tested by asking the patient to elevate the eye when it is fully
ADDUCTED (turned inwards)?
rationale: Inferior oblique elevates eye when fully adducted; Superior rectus elevates when abducted.

stem:
A patient with head tilt toward the left shoulder presents with vertical diplopia that worsens on downgaze
and dextroversion. Which cranial nerve is paralyzed?
rationale: 4th nerve palsy causes trochlear weakness, vertical diplopia, & compensatory head tilt.

stem:
A 40-year-old female presents with bilateral proptosis, lid retraction (Dalrymple's sign), lid lag on downgaze (Von
Graefe's sign), and restriction of extraocular movements. What is the diagnosis?
rationale: Thyroid Eye Disease presents with proptosis, Dalrymple sign (lid retraction), & Von Graefe sign.

stem:
Which extraocular muscle is most commonly involved and enlarged in Thyroid Eye Disease (Graves'
orbitopathy)?
rationale: Inferior rectus is most commonly involved muscle in Thyroid Eye Disease (IMSLO rule).

stem:
In ocular embryology, which germ layer gives rise to the crystalline lens, corneal epithelium, and lacrimal
gland (LEVL)?
rationale: Surface ectoderm gives rise to Lens, Epithelium, Vitreous, & Lacrimal gland (LEVL).

stem:
Which germ layer gives origin to the sphincter pupillae, dilator pupillae, and the sensory retina with its
RPE layer?
rationale: Neuroectoderm gives rise to Sphincter/Dilator pupillae, Retina, RPE, & Optic nerve.
